notation.meaning: Outcome: 1 log real hourly wage, 2 unemployment rate (%)
Difference-in-differences: Miami − comparison in $t_1$ minus the same in 1979

blocks.md: **About 125,000 Cubans arrived in Miami in mid-1980, raising its labor force by 7%. Relative to Atlanta, Houston, Los Angeles and Tampa–St. Petersburg, Miami's wages and unemployment show at most a small, short-lived deterioration over 1979–82: for blacks, the Miami−comparison gap in log wages was −0.15 in 1979, −0.23 in 1982 and −0.05 by 1985.**

sections.heading: Log real hourly earnings, workers aged 16–61 (Card Table 3)

blocks.md: Standard errors are about 0.02–0.06 in Miami and 0.01–0.03 in the comparison cities. Wages are deflated by the CPI (1980 = 100); the 1985 sample covers January–June only.

sections.heading: Differences and differences-in-differences (computed from Tables 3 and 4)

blocks.md: The first difference is Miami minus the comparison cities in a year; the difference-in-differences subtracts the 1979 first difference.
For whites the log-wage DiD stays within ±0.02 in every year; for Hispanics it is positive (0.04 to 0.12).

sections.heading: Who lived in Miami before the boatlift (Card Table 1, 1979)

blocks.md: The table describes Miami's residents before the boatlift. The lecture's point is that the Mariel Cubans' education and jobs resembled those of Miami's blacks, Cubans and other Hispanics more than its whites, so those are the groups most exposed to the new arrivals.

blocks.prompt: Pick a group and an outcome; move the comparison year to see the difference-in-differences against 1979.

blocks.md:
- **Not the immigrants' own outcomes.** Cubans in Miami include the new arrivals, so their wages fall partly because the group changed; there is no comparison-city Cuban series.
- **Only six post years and one pre year.** With data starting in 1979, parallel trends cannot be checked.
- **Noise.** Miami standard errors are 0.03 for log wages and 1–3 points for unemployment, so year-to-year swings of a few hundredths are within noise.
- **Common shocks.** Unemployment rose in the comparison cities too in 1982–83 (a national recession, beyond the lecture); the comparison cities absorb such common shocks.
